📚 Reference Links

  • Checkpointer versus store — thread-scoped state against cross-thread memory — LangGraph: persistence

  • The two together in one application, and when you need both — LangGraph: memory overview

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Short-term Working Memory — what sits in the window during a step, and offloading it.

  • State Management — checkpoints keyed to a thread id, and resuming from them.

  • Long-term Memory Taxonomy — the kinds of durable memory and what each is for.

What this note adds: the placement question those three notes each answer from their own side — given one piece of state, which store owns it, what its lifetime is, and what breaks when it lands in the wrong one. There is a fourth answer the memory notes don't cover, and it's usually the right one.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three stores and their lifetimes? Working context (per step) · thread state (per run) · long-term memory (per user).
The fourth answer people miss? Your actual database. Most "agent memory" is application state.
What keys thread state? A thread id; the checkpointer loads and resumes from it.
Cost of putting it in working context? Re-billed every step, so it compounds with steps².
The isolation rule? Long-term memory is per user, always. Cross-user leakage is the incident.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

For each piece of state I ask how long it must live and who owns it. If it's needed this step only, it goes in working context and I pay for it every subsequent step. If it must survive a crash within this run, it goes in thread state behind the checkpointer. If it must survive across sessions for one user, it goes in long-term memory with hard per-user isolation. And if it's a fact about the business rather than about the conversation, it belongs in the database it already belongs in — most things called agent memory are application state with a fashionable name.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Working context — in the window Needed by the model this step: the current tool result, the immediate plan. Re-billed every subsequent step; crowds the window and accelerates rot. The model must reason over it right now.
Thread state — checkpointer, per run Must survive a crash or a pause inside this run: step index, partial results, approvals. A store to run and a serialisation format to version. The run can be interrupted, resumed, or paused for a human.
Long-term memory — store, per user Must outlive the run: preferences, learned facts, prior outcomes. A write pipeline, a read policy, and a per-user isolation boundary to get right. "It should remember me next time."
The system of record — your database It's a business fact: an order, a ticket, an account. Nothing — you already run it. The cost is admitting the agent isn't special. Another service needs the same data, or it must be correct rather than recalled.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Working context Nothing new — but a compaction strategy becomes mandatory as steps accumulate. Directly drives the steps² term; the single biggest cost lever in the run. Watch window utilisation per step; rot shows up as quality decay late in long runs.
Thread state Adds a checkpointer and a durable store; makes resume and HITL pauses possible. Small per-step write. Buys back the cost of re-running a failed long run. Checkpoint size and write latency; a schema change now needs a migration path.
Long-term memory Adds write (extract, consolidate) and read (relevance, recency) pipelines plus a store. Two extra model calls per write if extraction is model-driven; retrieval per read. Per-user isolation is now a security control you must test, not a convention.
System of record An ordinary tool call against an existing service. Cheapest by far — no new infrastructure, no new failure mode. Nothing new. Existing ownership, backups and access control already apply.

The redraw test: the three agent stores are three different boxes with three different lifetimes. If your diagram has one box labelled "memory", you haven't made this decision — you've deferred it to whoever implements first.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why working context is the expensive answer. Anything you leave in the window is re-sent on every subsequent step. For a run of n steps, a block of t tokens placed at step 1 costs:

extra_input_tokens ≈ t × (n − 1)

A 4k-token document held across a twelve-step run is roughly 44k extra input tokens — for one document, on one run. That is the arithmetic behind "offload, don't hold": write it to thread state, keep a reference in the window, and re-read it only on the steps that need it.

The cheap test for whether it belongs in long-term memory. Ask whether a new run for the same user would be wrong without it. If yes, it's long-term memory. If it would merely be slower or need to ask again, it's probably fine to re-derive — and re-deriving has no isolation risk, no staleness, and no write pipeline to maintain.

The isolation number that matters. Cross-user leakage has no acceptable rate — it isn't a threshold to tune, so the design must make it structurally impossible: the user id is part of the store key, the read path can't express a query without it, and a test asserts a read for user A returns nothing written by user B. Cheap, and the one people skip.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. Does another service already own this fact? Ask first, because it eliminates most candidates. An order status is not agent memory; it's a query.

  2. Must it survive this run? No means working context or a thread-state scratchpad. Yes moves you down to the durable options.

  3. Is it about the user, or about the run? About the run means thread state keyed by thread id. About the user means long-term memory keyed by user id — and that key is the isolation boundary, so it isn't optional.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "A user saw a summary that mentioned another customer's account name."

Root cause. One memory store held everything — conversation facts, retrieved snippets, extracted entities — keyed by session, with user id a field on the record rather than part of the key. Retrieval was semantic. A support conversation about a similar problem scored highly, the user-id filter lived in application code that one retrieval path didn't apply, and another customer's fact entered the window and was summarised faithfully.

Fix. The store key became user-scoped so a cross-user read couldn't be expressed, and document snippets moved out of memory entirely — they were retrievable from the source and never needed persisting. The deeper fix was the placement question: three different kinds of state had been put in one store because it was the one labelled "memory", and only one of them belonged there.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You said most agent memory is application state. What do you actually mean?

That what teams reach for a vector store to remember is usually a record that already exists somewhere authoritative. Order status, subscription tier, ticket history — those live in a database, they're correct rather than approximate, and the agent should query them through a tool like any other client.

Memory earns its place for things with no system of record: that this user prefers terse answers, that a previous attempt at this task failed a particular way. Those are genuinely new facts produced by the interaction, which is the test I apply.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Thread state versus working context — if both survive the step, why not keep it in the window?

Because the window is re-billed. Something held in context costs tokens on every subsequent step, so a large item early in a long run is the dominant cost line, and it's also crowding out the material the model actually needs now. Thread state costs one write and one read when needed.

The trade is a round trip and some complexity — a reference in the window plus a tool to fetch it back. Not worth it for small items; the line is whether the item is large relative to what the step needs. For a plan or scratchpad the reference pattern wins comfortably; for a short fact it's noise.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

Long-term memory grows without bound. What happens at a year of usage per user?

Two things degrade differently. Retrieval quality falls first, because relevance scoring over tens of thousands of memories surfaces old near-duplicates — a consolidation problem, fixed by a write path that updates rather than appends, plus recency weighting at read.

Cost degrades more gently, since retrieval is bounded by top-k not store size. What I'd actually watch is staleness: a preference learned a year ago may be wrong, and nothing in a pure-append store expires it. So a decay or revalidation policy, and contradictions at write time treated as a signal to replace rather than store both — otherwise retrieval returns two conflicting facts and the model picks one arbitrarily.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the state layer for an agent platform where several teams' agents run for the same end user.

The shape I'd start from is one isolation boundary per user, shared across teams, with namespacing inside it. The user id is the outer key for everything durable, so a team's agent physically cannot read another user's data regardless of what its query says. Inside that boundary each agent namespaces its own memories, because one agent's learned facts are usually wrong for another's purpose — a billing agent's notion of "this user's preference" isn't the support agent's.

What I'd share is the write pipeline and the isolation test, not the memories. Extraction and consolidation are where the subtle bugs live; every team implementing their own is how one ends up storing raw transcripts. The platform runs that path and exposes it as an API.

Thread state stays per-run and per-agent — there's no case for sharing it, and sharing it would couple teams' state schemas together. The place cross-agent coordination belongs is explicit message passing or a blackboard the teams opt into, which is a different decision and has its own failure modes around concurrent writes.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We'll put it all in a vector store and retrieve what's relevant."

✅ Reality: That conflates four kinds of state with four lifetimes and four correctness requirements. Business facts need to be correct, not similar — semantic retrieval over them returns plausible answers, which is worse than no answer. Route by lifetime and ownership first, then pick a backend.

❌ Trap: "Long context windows make this decision go away."

✅ Reality: A bigger window changes what fits, not what it costs or how well the model attends to it. Everything in the window is re-billed per step and competes for attention; context rot is a quality problem, not a capacity one. A large window makes the wrong choice affordable for longer, which is not the same as correct.

❌ Trap: "User isolation is handled — we filter by user id on read."

✅ Reality: A filter is a line of code someone can forget on one of several read paths, which is exactly how leaks happen. Isolation should be structural: the user id belongs in the store key so an un-scoped read isn't expressible, with a test that asserts it.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • State Management — checkpointing, which is what makes thread state durable.

  • Long-term Memory Taxonomy — the kinds of durable memory once you've decided something is one.

  • Context engineering — the budget discipline for whatever you do leave in the window.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §7 Durable execution — thread state is what a checkpoint contains; this decides its size and shape.

  • §10 Cost modeling — working-context placement is the steps² term, so this is where that cost originates.

  • §11 Multi-tenant isolation — the long-term store's key is the tenancy boundary.

  • §5 Shared state across agents — only meaningful once each agent's own stores are settled.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent that takes actions — ticket history is a system of record, not memory, and saying so is the point.

  • §14 Deep research agent — findings held in the window are the classic steps² cost blow-up.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — the Tier 4 per-user boundary is the platform's core state decision.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Compaction, note-taking and just-in-time retrieval as the named strategies — Effective context engineering for AI agents (Anthropic)

  • Prompt caching, which decides where the static/dynamic split has to fall — Anthropic API: prompt caching

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Context engineering — what context engineering is and the techniques available.

  • Conversation Memory — summarisation versus windowing, and summary drift.

What this note adds: the eviction order. The concept note lists the techniques; this decides which one you apply first when the window fills, what each costs you in fidelity, and why the order is forced by prefix caching rather than chosen freely.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The eviction order? Tool results → old turns → retrieved docs → the plan. Never the system prompt.
Why that order? Cheapest to re-fetch goes first; hardest to reconstruct goes last.
What forces the layout? Prefix caching — static content first, or you invalidate the cache every step.
The trap in summarisation? Lossy and compounding; each pass re-summarises a summary.
What replaces holding? A reference plus a fetch tool — just-in-time retrieval.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Context is a budget, so the real question is what I evict first when it fills. My order is tool results, then old turns, then retrieved documents, then — last and reluctantly — the working plan. The principle is cheapest-to-reconstruct goes first: a tool result I can re-fetch, a document I can re-retrieve, but a plan the model built over ten steps is expensive to rebuild and losing it causes the agent to wander. The layout itself is forced by prefix caching: static content first, dynamic last, or I invalidate the cache on every step and pay full price for the whole prefix.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Trim oldest-first Conversational agents where recent turns dominate relevance. Drops facts established early — the user's original constraint disappears. Long chat, shallow tool use.
Summarise The history matters but its detail doesn't. Lossy and compounding — each pass summarises a summary, and specifics erode first. Long runs where "what we decided" matters more than "what was said".
Offload + reference Large artifacts: documents, files, long tool outputs. A round trip when it's needed again, and a tool to fetch it. Any single item that's large relative to what the step needs.
Just-in-time retrieval The agent can identify what it needs by name or id. Retrieval latency per step, and the risk of fetching the wrong thing. The material is in a store the agent can query anyway.
Sub-agent isolation A subtask needs a lot of context the parent doesn't. Coordination cost and a handoff where context is lost. One branch is drowning the shared window.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Trim Nothing — a window policy in the harness. Cheapest. Bounded input per step. Watch for "it forgot what I said at the start" complaints.
Summarise Adds a summarisation call and a place to store the rolling summary. An extra model call per compaction; cheaper than carrying the history. Summary drift becomes a quality signal — sample them.
Offload + reference Adds a scratchpad store and a fetch tool; the window holds pointers. Removes the t × (n−1) re-billing for that item; adds one fetch when needed. Store lifecycle — when do scratchpads get cleaned up?
JIT retrieval Retrieval becomes a tool in the loop rather than a preprocessing step. Per-step retrieval cost; less waste than carrying everything. Retrieval quality now affects every step, not just the first.
Sub-agent isolation A second agent with its own window and a defined return contract. Multiplies tokens; the parent pays for the summary that comes back. Handoff loss becomes a failure mode you have to look for.

The redraw test: offloading and JIT retrieval both put a store and a fetch tool in the diagram. Trimming and summarising don't — they're policies, not boxes. Knowing which you chose tells someone whether the picture is complete.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why order matters more than technique. Anything carried in the window is re-billed each step, so a block of t tokens across n steps costs t × (n − 1) extra input tokens. Evicting a 4k tool result at step 2 of a twelve-step run saves ~40k input tokens; evicting the 200-token plan saves 2k and costs you the run's coherence. The order follows directly from that ratio — evict big-and-cheap-to-refetch, keep small-and-expensive-to-rebuild.

The caching constraint that fixes the layout. Prompt caching keys on an exact prefix match, so any edit invalidates everything after the edit point. That means static content — system prompt, tool definitions, stable instructions — must sit at the front and never change mid-run, with all mutation confined to the tail. Getting this backwards, by putting a rolling summary before the tool definitions, invalidates the cache on every compaction and quietly doubles input cost on exactly the long runs you were trying to optimise.

The threshold to act on. Compact at a fraction of the window, not at the limit — the model needs room to produce output, and hitting the ceiling mid-step is a hard failure rather than a degradation. A workable rule is to compact when the prompt exceeds roughly two-thirds of the window, measured per step, and to alarm if compaction fires more than once per run, because that means the step is carrying more than it should.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. What is actually biggest? Measure before choosing a technique. It's usually one tool result or one document, not the conversation everyone assumes.

  2. Can I get it back? If yes, offload it — that's strictly better than summarising, because it's lossless.

  3. Do the details still matter? Only when they don't is summarisation safe, and even then it compounds across passes.

  4. Am I compacting every run? Then the answer isn't a better compaction strategy — it's fewer steps.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Long conversations get vague, and then it starts contradicting things the user told it."

Root cause. The harness summarised the whole history whenever the prompt crossed a threshold, including previous summaries. By the fourth compaction the model was reading a summary of a summary of a summary, and concrete constraints — a date, a budget figure, an excluded vendor — had been abstracted away into "the user has some requirements". Nothing was wrong with any single summarisation; the loss was compounding, and the rolling summary also sat before the tool definitions, so every compaction invalidated the prefix cache and the cost rose as the quality fell.

Fix. Constraints were extracted once into a small structured block that was never summarised, the rolling summary moved after the static prefix, and large tool results were offloaded to a scratchpad with references in the window. The general lesson is that summarisation is the only lossy option on the list, so it should be the last one reached for and never applied to its own output.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

You said evict tool results first. Aren't those the most relevant thing in the window?

The most recent one usually is, and I'd keep it. What I evict is the accumulated tail — the result from step two that's still being re-sent at step eleven because nothing removed it. That's the bulk of the window in most long runs, and it's the cheapest thing to lose because the agent can call the tool again.

The distinction I'd make explicit is between the result I'm reasoning over right now and the transcript of everything I've ever fetched. Harnesses accumulate the second by default, and that accumulation is what the budget is actually being spent on.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Summarisation versus offloading — why is offloading strictly better when it's available?

Because it's lossless and reversible. An offloaded document is byte-identical when fetched back; a summarised one has lost whatever the summariser judged unimportant, and that judgement was made without knowing what the agent would need later. The cost difference is a round trip against a permanent loss of fidelity.

Offloading isn't always available, which is when summarisation earns its place — a conversation has no external store to point at, and you can't re-fetch what the user said. So the real rule is: offload anything that has a source, summarise only what doesn't.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

The agent now runs for two hours across hundreds of steps. Does any of this still hold?

The order holds but the strategy changes, because at that length no compaction policy keeps a single window coherent — context rot sets in regardless of how carefully you trim. The shape that works is periodic fresh starts: the agent writes durable state to a store, then a new context is opened seeded only with the plan, the constraints, and the current step's inputs.

That makes the plan the load-bearing artifact rather than the transcript, which is why the plan is last in the eviction order. It also changes what you monitor — steps-since-restart and quality against restart boundary, rather than window utilisation. The failure I'd watch for is a restart that loses something the transcript held implicitly, which is an argument for extracting constraints into explicit state early rather than trusting they'll survive.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design the context layer so several agents with different budgets share one implementation.

I'd make the window a composed artifact rather than an accumulated one — each step assembles the prompt from named segments with declared roles, rather than appending to a growing list. Segments carry a priority and a reconstructability flag, and the assembler evicts by those attributes when the budget is exceeded. That turns eviction order from a per-agent policy into a property of the segment.

The layout constraint is enforced by the assembler rather than by convention: static segments are ordered first and marked immutable for the run, so no team can accidentally put a rolling summary ahead of the tool definitions and destroy caching for everyone. Cache hit rate per agent becomes the metric that tells you whether the discipline is holding.

What I'd expose per agent is the budget and the segment priorities, not the mechanism. Teams get to say "the plan is critical, retrieved docs are disposable" and the platform decides what that means in tokens, which keeps the eviction logic in one place where it can be tested.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "The window is 200k tokens, so context management isn't a concern for us."

✅ Reality: Window size sets what fits, not what it costs or how well the model attends. Every token is re-billed per step and competes for attention. A big window lets you defer the decision, which usually means discovering it as a cost spike rather than a design choice.

❌ Trap: "We summarise when the context gets long — that's our context engineering."

✅ Reality: Summarisation is the lossiest option on the menu and the only one that compounds. It should be the last technique reached for, never applied to its own output, and never applied to constraints the user stated explicitly.

❌ Trap: "Put the conversation first so the model sees the most important thing early."

✅ Reality: Prefix caching keys on an exact prefix, so anything mutable placed early invalidates the cache for everything after it. Static content goes first for cost reasons; recency is handled by position within the dynamic tail, not by moving the tail to the front.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Context engineering — the techniques this note sequences.

  • Short-term Working Memory — offloading, which is the preferred eviction.

  • caching in agentic systems — why the static/dynamic split is forced.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §5 Which store holds this state — offloading is that decision applied under pressure.

  • §5 Context rot — compaction policy is what determines how fast rot arrives.

  • §10 Caching tiers — the layout this note forces is what makes prefix caching possible at all.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — findings accumulate, so eviction order is the whole cost story.

  • §14 Coding agent — repo context is large and re-fetchable, which makes it the textbook offload case.

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Sub-agent context isolation and fresh-context restarts as the production answer to long runs — How we built our multi-agent research system (Anthropic)

  • Why retrieval quality degrades as context grows, independent of window size — Lost in the Middle: how language models use long contexts (arXiv 2307.03172)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Context Rot — what rot and poisoning are, and why long runs degrade.

  • Manager Sub-agent Delegation — how a sub-agent's isolated context is set up and returned.

What this note adds: the intervention choice. The concept note diagnoses rot; this decides what you do about it — compact harder, restart fresh, or isolate in a sub-agent — and the signal that tells you which, before quality visibly drops.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The three interventions? Compact harder · restart with fresh context · isolate in a sub-agent.
What restarts cost? Everything implicit in the transcript. Only explicit state survives.
Poisoning vs rot? Rot is degradation with length; poisoning is a bad fact that persists and spreads.
The early signal? Repeated or near-identical tool calls — the agent has lost track of what it did.
Why a bigger window doesn't fix it? Attention degrades with length; rot is a quality problem, not a capacity one.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Long runs degrade, and I treat that as a design parameter, not a surprise. Under about a dozen steps I just compact. Past that I plan for a fresh context: the agent writes its plan and findings to durable state, and a new window is seeded with only those — which works precisely because I decided earlier what was explicit state rather than transcript. If one branch generates most of the context, I isolate it in a sub-agent so the parent never sees the volume. The thing that forces the choice is poisoning: once a wrong fact is in the window, compaction preserves it and only a restart removes it.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Compact harder Short-to-medium runs where the window is merely full. Preserves whatever is wrong along with whatever is right. Lossy if summarising. Window pressure but coherent behaviour.
Fresh-context restart Long runs, or any run where a bad fact has taken hold. Everything implicit in the transcript is gone — only explicit state survives. Repeated tool calls, drifting plan, contradictions with earlier turns.
Sub-agent isolation One subtask produces far more context than the rest. Token multiplication and a handoff where nuance is lost. One branch dominating the window while others sit idle.
Cut the step count Compaction fires on every run. Scope reduction — you're delivering less per run. You're compacting as routine rather than as exception.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Compact A policy in the harness; no new components. Cheap per compaction; the accumulated context keeps being re-billed. Watch quality across run length — rot is invisible until it isn't.
Restart Forces a durable state store and an explicit re-seed contract. Resets the per-step input cost; adds one state write and read per restart. Steps-since-restart becomes a live metric; so does quality at restart boundaries.
Sub-agent A second agent, a delegation contract, and a return format. Multiplies tokens on that branch; the parent pays only for the summary. Handoff loss is a new failure class to look for in traces.
Fewer steps Usually a workflow shape replacing part of the loop. The largest saving available, because cost grows with steps². Less to operate. The design conversation moves back to §1.

The redraw test: restarting puts a durable state store and a re-seed path in the diagram; sub-agent isolation puts a second agent box in it. Compaction alone changes nothing visible, which is why teams reach for it and then wonder why the picture never improved.

5. 🔢 The Numbers

Why length itself is the problem. Lost in the Middle showed that model performance on retrieving a fact depends on where it sits in the context, with material in the middle recovered least reliably and the effect worsening as context grows. So a fact that entered at step three is not merely still present at step twenty — it is present in the least-attended region. That is rot: nothing was deleted, and the model still can't use it.

The restart budget. A restart costs one state write plus one re-seed read, and resets per-step input to the seed size. For a run at twelve steps carrying 30k tokens of accumulated context, continuing costs roughly 30k per step; restarting with a 3k seed costs 3k per step from there. The break-even is immediate — the question is never whether restarting is cheaper, it's whether the seed captures enough.

The signal to act on, before quality drops. Repeated or near-identical tool calls are the earliest reliable indicator, because they mean the agent has lost track of what it already did. That is countable in the trace without any judgement call, so it makes a good alarm: alert when a run issues the same tool with the same arguments more than once, and treat a rising rate across runs as the cue to lower the restart threshold.

6. 🧭 The Decision Procedure

The questions, in order:

  1. Is something in the window wrong? Poisoning changes the answer entirely, because every compaction faithfully carries the bad fact forward. Only a restart from clean state removes it.

  2. Where is the volume coming from? If one branch dominates, isolate that rather than penalising the whole run.

  3. Is this every run or the tail? Routine compaction means the run is too long for its shape, and the fix belongs back at the control-flow decision.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It decided early that a library was deprecated, and everything after that was built around avoiding it — including after we told it otherwise."

Root cause. A stale search result in an early step asserted the deprecation. The claim entered the window as a tool result and the agent reasoned from it correctly, so nothing looked broken. Every compaction preserved it, because compaction summarises what's present rather than validating it, and by the time a later step returned contradicting evidence the wrong fact had been restated in several derived conclusions and carried more weight than the correction. The window contained both, and the model resolved the conflict toward the version repeated most.

Fix. A restart threshold, and a rule that findings promoted into the re-seed must carry their source step so a contradiction can be traced. The structural lesson is that poisoning is not a compaction bug to be tuned away — compaction has no notion of truth, so the only intervention that removes a bad fact is dropping the context that contains it.

8. 🎤 How It's Probed

Tier 1 — Clarification

What actually survives a restart?

Only what was written to durable state before it. That's the plan, any findings explicitly promoted, the constraints, and the step index. Everything implicit in the transcript — the reasoning that led somewhere, a preference inferred from phrasing, the fact that an approach was already tried and abandoned — is gone.

Which is why the restart decision is really made much earlier, when you decide what gets extracted into state versus left in the window. An agent that never promoted anything can't be restarted safely, so the shape has to be designed in from the start rather than added when runs get long.

Tier 2 — Trade-off

Sub-agent isolation versus restarting — both drop context. When does each win?

Isolation wins when the volume is localised: one deep subtask generating a lot of material the rest of the run doesn't need. The parent stays coherent throughout and pays only for the returned summary, so there's no discontinuity in the main line of reasoning.

Restarting wins when the volume is diffuse — everything has grown, nothing branch is obviously at fault — or when something is wrong and has to go. Isolation can't help with poisoning in the parent, because the bad fact is in the window you're keeping.

The cost profile differs too. Isolation multiplies tokens, since the sub-agent re-reads its own context each step; restarting reduces them. So if the driver is cost rather than coherence, restart is the lever.

Tier 3 — Edge case / scaling

At two hours and hundreds of steps, how do you keep quality stable rather than merely non-zero?

I'd stop treating it as one run. The shape becomes a sequence of bounded episodes with durable state between them, where each episode is short enough that rot doesn't set in — a dozen steps or so — and the state carried across is a deliberate, small artifact rather than a transcript.

That forces a genuine plan representation: a structured object with steps, status and findings, updated as the run proceeds. It's what makes an episode boundary safe and what someone debugging at hour two actually reads. It also localises drift detection — a plan that hasn't advanced across two episodes is a stuck run whatever the model is saying.

The metric is quality against episode index — if episode five is worse than episode one, the seed is losing something and the fix is in what gets promoted, not in episode length.

Tier 4 — Open-ended design

Design a long-running agent where rot is prevented structurally rather than managed.

I'd invert the default: instead of accumulating context and evicting under pressure, each step assembles the window from explicit state plus only what that step needs. Nothing persists in the window by default, so there is no accumulation to rot. The transcript still exists for audit, but it isn't the working memory.

That makes the state object the centre of the design — plan, findings with provenance, constraints, and the current subtask. Steps read from it and write to it, and the prompt is a projection of it. The cost is that the model can't rely on having seen the history, so every step's inputs have to be complete, which is real work per tool and per step.

What it buys is that run length stops being a quality variable: a step at hour two has the same window shape as one at minute one, and poisoning becomes tractable because a wrong finding is a record you invalidate rather than a sentence buried in a transcript. I'd watch state growth instead — findings accumulate, so promotion needs its own budget and eviction rule.

9. ⚠️ Traps & Misconceptions

❌ Trap: "We moved to a million-token model, so rot is solved."

✅ Reality: Capacity and attention are different. Lost in the Middle showed retrieval quality depends on position and degrades with length; a larger window moves the ceiling without changing the gradient. It lets you accumulate more before noticing, which usually means noticing later and more expensively.

❌ Trap: "Compaction handles poisoning — the bad fact gets summarised away."

✅ Reality: Compaction has no notion of truth. It preserves what's salient, and a fact the agent has reasoned from repeatedly is highly salient. Summarising a poisoned context produces a compact poisoned context.

❌ Trap: "Restarts lose context, so they're a last resort."

✅ Reality: They lose implicit context, which is exactly the part you can't rely on anyway in a long run. If the explicit state is good enough to restart from, it was good enough to be reasoning from all along — and if it isn't, that's the real defect.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Context Rot — the diagnosis this note responds to.

  • Manager Sub-agent Delegation — the isolation option, in full.

  • Planning failure modes — drift, which is what rot looks like from the plan's side.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §5 What gets cut when the window fills — compaction is the option this note often rejects.

  • §5 Which store holds this state — restarts are only safe if state placement was decided well.

  • §6 Orchestrator-worker topology — sub-agent isolation is the context-driven reason to go multi-agent.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — hours-long runs make episode boundaries mandatory.

  • §14 Coding agent — a wrong early conclusion about the codebase is the canonical poisoning case.

notes.title: Whether to build a long-term memory pipeline at all
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§5 Memory, State & Context)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Relevance + recency + importance scoring, and reflection as consolidation — Generative Agents: interactive simulacra of human behavior (arXiv 2304.03442)

  • The store as cross-thread memory, separate from the checkpointer — LangGraph: memory overview

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Memory Write — extraction and the add/update/delete consolidation decision.

  • Memory Read — relevance, recency and decay scoring at read time.

What this note adds: the build-or-skip fork those two notes assume you've already passed. They describe a pipeline worth building; this asks whether yours is, and names the three cheaper substitutes that cover most cases.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The test for needing it? A new run for the same user is wrong without it. Not merely slower.
The cheapest substitute? An explicit user-editable preferences record. No extraction, no drift.
What the pipeline really costs? Two model calls per write, plus an isolation boundary you must test.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

Most agents don't need one. The test I apply is whether a fresh run for the same user would be wrong without the memory, not merely slower or more repetitive — if it would just ask again, that's acceptable and free. When something genuinely must persist, I reach for an explicit preferences record before a learned-memory pipeline, because it's user-visible, correctable, and has no extraction step to get wrong. I build extract-consolidate-read-forget only when the facts worth keeping are ones the user wouldn't think to state, which is a narrower case than it first looks.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
No memory — re-derive each run The agent can ask, or the context is in the request. Repetition the user notices, and a slightly longer first turn. Sessions are self-contained; each task stands alone.
Explicit preferences record The durable facts are ones a user would state if asked. A settings surface to build. Nothing is learned automatically. "Remember I prefer X" is the whole requirement.
Summary per user Continuity matters more than precision — tone, history, rapport. Lossy and drifts; no provenance for any single claim. A long-running assistant relationship, low stakes per fact.
Full pipeline — extract, consolidate, read, forget Facts worth keeping emerge from behaviour and the user wouldn't volunteer them. Two model calls per write, a store, a read policy, and an isolation boundary to test. Personalisation is the product, not a convenience.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
No memory Nothing. Zero. Nothing to isolate, so no cross-user risk at all.
Preferences record An ordinary table and a settings UI. Negligible — one read per run. Standard data ownership; users can correct it themselves.
Summary per user A store plus a summarisation call at session end. One call per session; one read per run. Drift and staleness; no way to correct a single wrong belief.
Full pipeline Write path (extract, consolidate), read path (relevance, recency), store, per-user key. ~2 model calls per write, retrieval per read, plus storage growth. Isolation is now a security control with a test; staleness needs a decay policy.

The redraw test: the first two add no agent-specific boxes at all. Only the fourth adds a write pipeline, and if your diagram has one, you should be able to say what it learns that a user wouldn't just tell you.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "It keeps insisting I work in the Frankfurt office. I moved eighteen months ago and I've corrected it twice."

Root cause. The pipeline extracted facts and appended them, with consolidation limited to near-duplicate detection on text similarity. "Works in Frankfurt" and "moved to Lisbon" aren't textually similar, so both were stored, and the older memory had accrued more retrieval hits — which the read scoring treated as importance. Corrections created new memories instead of invalidating old ones, so each attempt made the store more confident in the wrong answer.

Fix. Consolidation moved from similarity to contradiction — a write that conflicts with an existing memory on the same attribute replaces it rather than joining it — and memories gained a source and a timestamp so recency could break ties. The broader lesson is that append-only memory is not a simpler version of memory; it's a store that gets worse the longer it runs.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Memory Write — the write path, once you've decided to build one.

  • Memory Read — scoring, which is where staleness is either handled or isn't.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §5 Which store holds this state — this is that note's third branch, examined on its own.

  • §11 Multi-tenant isolation — a memory store's key is a tenancy boundary.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Support agent — prior ticket history is a system of record, not learned memory; saying so avoids the whole pipeline.

  • §14 Voice / interview agent — cross-session continuity is where the pipeline genuinely earns its place.

notes.title: Retrieval as a tool, or a fixed pipeline before the model
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§5 Memory, State & Context)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Retrieval promoted to an agent-controlled action, and when that earns its cost — Agentic RAG survey (arXiv 2501.09136)

  • Self-grading retrieval and the corrective re-query loop — Corrective Retrieval Augmented Generation (arXiv 2401.15884)

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Agentic RAG — Retrieval as an Agent-Controlled Tool — what agentic RAG is and how the tool is wired.

  • self-correcting retrieval loops — agent grades and re-retrieves — the grade-and-re-retrieve mechanism.

What this note adds: the fork the index bullet names and those notes assume away — when a fixed pipeline is enough. The cost of agentic retrieval is a variable number of retrieval rounds per answer, and most questions don't need more than one.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What promotes retrieval to a tool? The query you need can't be written until you've seen earlier results.
What it costs? Variable rounds per answer — latency and cost stop being predictable.
The cheap middle option? Fixed pipeline plus one grade-and-retry, not a full loop.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I default to a fixed pipeline — retrieve once, rerank, answer — because for most questions a single well-formed query is enough and the cost is predictable. Retrieval becomes a tool only when the second query genuinely depends on what the first returned: multi-hop questions, or ones where the right corpus isn't known up front. The cheap middle I reach for first is a fixed pipeline with one grading step and at most one retry, which catches the "retrieved nothing useful" case without opening an unbounded loop. Unbounded re-retrieval is where latency budgets quietly die.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Fixed pipeline One query answers it; the corpus is known. No recovery when retrieval misses — the model answers from bad context. Questions are self-contained and look like the documents.
Fixed + grade + one retry Mostly single-hop, but a miss is expensive. One extra grading call, and one extra retrieval on the miss path. Occasional "it answered from the wrong document" complaints.
Retrieval as a tool (agentic) The next query depends on the last result; multi-hop or multi-corpus. Rounds per answer become variable — p95 and cost stop being predictable. "Compare X and Y across sources", or the corpus is chosen by the question.
Query planning up front The decomposition is knowable from the question alone. A planning call, and brittleness if the plan was wrong. Questions decompose cleanly and predictably into sub-questions.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Fixed Retrieval is a preprocessing step, outside the loop. One retrieval per answer. Fully predictable p95. Retrieval quality measured offline on a fixed set.
Fixed + retry Adds a grader between retrieval and generation. One extra call always, one extra retrieval sometimes. Retry rate becomes the health signal for retrieval quality.
Agentic Retrieval joins the tool layer; needs a round cap and per-round tracing. Multiplies by rounds; context grows with each result kept. You now trace retrieval decisions, not just retrieval results.
Query planning A planner node before a parallel fan-out of retrievals. Planning call plus N parallel retrievals — latency of the slowest. Plan quality is a separate thing to evaluate from retrieval quality.

The redraw test: fixed retrieval sits outside the loop; agentic retrieval sits inside it as a tool. That single move is what changes cost from predictable to variable.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Some answers take four seconds and some take forty, on questions that look identical to users."

Root cause. Retrieval had been made a tool so the agent could re-query when results looked thin, with no cap on rounds. For most questions it retrieved once. For questions where the corpus genuinely lacked an answer, the agent kept rephrasing and re-retrieving — each round returning plausible-but-unhelpful chunks that scored well enough to justify another attempt. The loop wasn't broken; it was correctly persisting on a question the corpus couldn't answer, and nothing told it to stop.

Fix. A hard cap of three retrieval rounds, and an explicit abstention path — after the cap, the agent answers "the sources don't cover this" rather than continuing. Abstention turned out to be the more valuable half: without it the agent had no way to express failure, so it kept searching rather than admitting a gap.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Iterative & Multi-hop Retrieval Driven by the Agent — the multi-hop case that justifies the tool.

  • Query Planning & Decomposition for Retrieval — the fourth option here, in full.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §8 Hard budgets — agentic retrieval needs a round cap, which is where it comes from.

  • §5 What gets cut when the window fills — each retained retrieval round is window pressure.

  • §9 Latency — variable rounds are usually the largest single source of p95 spread.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — the case where agentic retrieval is unambiguously right.

  • §14 Support agent — usually fixed-plus-retry; unbounded search on a closed knowledge base wastes budget.

notes.title: Shared blackboard or message passing between agents
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§5 Memory, State & Context)

headings.text: ⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)
🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)
🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • Handoffs as explicit message passing, with the contract at the boundary — OpenAI Agents SDK: handoffs

  • Shared graph state and what concurrent branch writes do to it — LangGraph: persistence

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Agent Communication — the communication mechanisms and their shapes.

  • Coordination Problems — duplicated work, conflicting writes, lost context at handoff.

What this note adds: the fork between the two shapes and the concurrency consequence nobody draws — a blackboard is shared mutable state between non-deterministic writers, which is a race with an LLM holding the pen.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
The two shapes? Blackboard (shared mutable state) vs message passing (explicit handoff payloads).
The blackboard's real cost? Concurrent writes from non-deterministic agents — last-write-wins on a guess.
Default for parallel sub-agents? Message passing: each returns a payload; the parent merges deliberately.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

I default to message passing — each sub-agent returns a typed payload and the orchestrator merges, so every write to shared state happens in one place under code I control. A blackboard is tempting because it looks like less plumbing, but it's shared mutable state with several non-deterministic writers, and the merge conflicts don't announce themselves: two agents update the same field, last write wins, and nothing in the trace says a decision was overwritten. I'd use a blackboard only when agents genuinely need to observe each other's partial progress mid-run, and then with append-only entries rather than mutable fields.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Message passing Parallel sub-agents with independent subtasks — the production default. Nothing shared, so no cross-agent visibility until the merge. Orchestrator-worker shape; each worker's job is self-contained.
Blackboard (mutable) Agents must react to each other's partial results as they arrive. Concurrent writes with no conflict semantics; silent overwrites. "They need to see what the others found."
Blackboard (append-only) Same need, but you want the conflicts to be visible. Readers must reconcile contradictory entries; the log grows. Shared findings where disagreement is informative.
Shared external store State must outlive the run or be read by non-agent consumers. A real datastore with real transaction semantics — and the latency of one. Another service consumes the output too.

4. 📐 What It Flips

If you choose Architecture changes Budget changes Ops changes
Message passing A return contract per sub-agent; merge logic in the orchestrator. The parent pays for each returned payload in its own window. Handoff loss is the failure to watch — what the payload didn't carry.
Blackboard (mutable) One shared state object all agents write; needs a write policy you must invent. Cheap to write, but every reader re-reads the whole board into context. Silent overwrites. You'll need write provenance to debug anything.
Blackboard (append-only) Shared log plus a reconciliation step before use. The log itself becomes window pressure as it grows. Contradiction rate becomes a signal worth watching.
External store A database with transactions; agents become ordinary clients. Store latency per access; no token cost for what isn't read. Standard data ops — and standard concurrency control, which is the point.

The redraw test: message passing draws arrows between agents; a blackboard draws a box they all point at. If the box is there, someone has to answer what happens when two arrows arrive at once.

7. 💥 Failure Story

Symptom. "Two of the three sub-agents did the same work, and the final report cited one source twice as if it were two."

Root cause. Three research sub-agents shared a blackboard holding a findings list and a covered_topics field. Each was supposed to check covered_topics before starting and update it after. They ran in parallel, all read the field before any had written, all chose the topic that looked most central, and two wrote overlapping findings. The dedupe at merge time compared text rather than source ids, so near-identical findings from the same document survived as separate citations. Nothing errored: the coordination protocol existed, it just assumed sequential execution.

Fix. Topic assignment moved to the orchestrator before dispatch — workers were told what to cover rather than choosing — and findings carried source ids so dedupe had something exact to compare. The general lesson is that a shared field read-then-written by parallel agents is a classic race, and the fix is the ordinary one: make the assignment in a single place rather than coordinating through shared state.

10. 🔗 Connections

⬆️ Depends on (concepts assumed)

  • Coordination Problems — the failure classes this fork chooses between.

  • Orchestrator-Worker Pattern — where message passing is the natural shape.

🔁 Decides / constrains (other decisions this one forces)

  • §6 Orchestrator-worker — the delegation contract is the message-passing payload.

  • §5 Which store holds this state — shared state is only coherent once each agent's own stores are settled.

  • §4 Parallel tool calls — the same race, one layer down.

🏗️ Design problems that hinge on this

  • §14 Deep research agent — parallel searchers are exactly this decision.

  • §14 Internal agent platform — cross-team agents sharing state is where isolation and coordination collide.

notes.title: Which memory backend, and whether to adopt a framework
notes.category: Agentic System Design (§5 Memory, State & Context)
notes.html:
📚 Reference Links

  • The store abstraction most frameworks expose, and what it assumes of the backend — LangGraph: memory overview

0. 🔒 Owned Elsewhere

Concepts assumed (don't re-read unless rusty):

  • Memory Backends — vector, key-value and graph stores and what each is good at.

  • Memory Frameworks — Mem0, Zep, Letta and what they provide.

What this note adds: the one-line placement — that the backend follows from the read pattern, and that adopting a framework is a build-vs-buy call on the pipeline, not on the store.

1. 🎯 Recall Check

Prompt Answer (cover this column)
What picks the backend? The read pattern: key → KV · similarity → vector · relationship → graph.
What a memory framework sells you? The extract-consolidate-read pipeline, not storage.

2. The Decision in 30 Seconds

The backend falls out of how you read. Fetch a user's preferences by id and it's a key-value store — most "agent memory" is this, and a vector database is over-engineering. Find things by similarity and it's a vector store. Traverse relationships between entities and it's a graph. A memory framework is a different decision: it sells you the write and read pipeline, which is the genuinely fiddly part, so adopt one if you've decided you need that pipeline and don't want to own extraction and consolidation yourself.

3. 🔱 The Fork

Option Choose when What it costs you Tell-tale signal
Key-value Reads are by user id or thread id. No similarity search — you must know what you're asking for. "Load this user's preferences."
Vector Reads are "what's relevant to this". Approximate, and relevance isn't correctness. Free-text recall over past interactions.
Graph Reads traverse relationships between entities. Extraction into a schema, which is real work and drifts. "How is X connected to Y?"
Managed framework You need the full pipeline and don't want to own it. A dependency on someone else's memory model and its failure modes. Personalisation is the product and the team is small.
